title: Remedies under the HRA
subtitle: Victims, 'just satisfaction' and choosing the right toolkit
objectives: State the s 7 'victim' requirement and explain how it differs from standing in ordinary judicial review
Explain why s 8 damages follow the Strasbourg 'just satisfaction' approach rather than tort-measure compensation, and identify when a declaration of incompatibility is used instead
Compare HRA remedies with judicial review remedies and select the right toolkit for a given complaint

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory remedial framework: who can sue, and what a court can award

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Greenfield) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] UKHL 14
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms s 8 damages follow the Strasbourg 'just satisfaction' approach, not tort principles

leadingAuthorities.citation: Anufrijeva v Southwark LBC [2003] EWCA Civ 1406
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes damages as a remedy of last resort under the HRA

leadingAuthorities.citation: Faulkner v Secretary of State for Justice [2013] UKSC 23
leadingAuthorities.role: Refines quantum guidance, aligning domestic awards more closely with Strasbourg practice

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students who can state s 6 and the Convention rights fluently often stumble the moment a problem question asks 'what remedy?' — because the HRA's remedies are deliberately modest and easy to over-claim. This lesson is where knowing the right is tested against knowing what winning is actually worth.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the sections. The test pool below leans on scenarios where you have to pick between damages, a declaration of incompatibility, and ordinary judicial review relief — that's the actual exam skill here.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Parts 1 and 2 before the comparisons start. If s 7 and s 8 aren't solid, the rest of the lesson will feel like it's built on sand.

overview.hook: A claimant proves, beyond argument, that a public authority breached their Article 8 rights. They expect a cheque. Instead the court finds the breach, says so in a judgment, and awards nothing — because under the HRA, being right and being paid are two separate questions, and the second one is answered far more stingily than most students expect.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This is a settled statutory and case-law framework; no legislative change to ss 7–8 is pending.

parts.heading: Who can even bring a claim: the s 7 victim test
parts.voice: practical — treats the section as a gatekeeping filter before anything about merits
body: Before any question of remedy arises, s 7(1) HRA asks a narrower question than most students expect: is the claimant a 'victim' of the alleged unlawful act? This is deliberately tighter than the 'sufficient interest' test for standing in ordinary judicial review, where a well-organised pressure group can often bring a claim about a public wrong even if no member has been personally affected.

Section 7(7) imports the Strasbourg 'victim' test directly: a person must be directly affected, or — in limited circumstances, such as a close relative bringing a claim after a death — an indirect victim. A campaigning organisation cannot bring a free-standing HRA claim purely in the public interest, however strong its evidence of systemic wrongdoing; it can join judicial review proceedings as an interested party or intervener, but it cannot itself be 'the victim'.

This matters practically: a lawyer spotting a strong Convention argument in a case with no clear personal victim should be thinking judicial review — where standing is generous — rather than a free-standing HRA claim, where it is not. The two systems run side by side, and the HRA route is the narrower gate.

components.definition: A person directly affected by the act complained of, interpreted in line with Article 34 Strasbourg case law — narrower than 'sufficient interest' for standing in judicial review, and generally excluding organisations acting purely in a representative or public-interest capacity.

interaction.prompt: A civil liberties charity, with no member personally affected, wants to bring a free-standing HRA claim about a policy it says breaches Article 8 across the board. Can it satisfy the s 7 victim test on its own?
options: No — the charity itself is not a 'victim' unless directly or indirectly affected
Yes — any organisation with relevant expertise can bring an HRA claim in the public interest
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The s 7 gate is narrower than judicial review standing precisely so it tracks the Strasbourg individual-complaint model — the charity would need to intervene in, or support, a claim brought by an actual victim.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — s 7(7) imports the Strasbourg 'victim' concept, which is markedly narrower than 'sufficient interest'. A representative body with no personally affected claimant cannot bring a free-standing HRA claim alone.

parts.heading: s 8 damages: 'just satisfaction', not compensation
parts.voice: comparative — sets tort damages up as the wrong mental model, then corrects it
body: Section 8(3)–(4) is the section that most disappoints claimants in practice. It does not create a free-standing right to damages for every proven breach. A court may award damages only if it is necessary to afford 'just satisfaction' to the person affected, and only after considering any other relief already granted (a declaration, a quashing order) and the consequences of any decision.

Crucially, s 8(4) requires the court to take into account the principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights when awarding just satisfaction under Article 41 of the Convention. Strasbourg awards are notoriously modest compared with English tort damages — a finding of a breach is often treated, on its own, as sufficient vindication, with no additional sum awarded at all.

This is why the leading case, R (Greenfield) v SSHD, matters so much: the House of Lords held explicitly that domestic courts should not import tort measures of damages (loss of amenity, exemplary damages, the full common-law toolkit) into s 8 awards. The comparator is Strasbourg's own jurisprudence, not the tort tables a common lawyer instinctively reaches for.

components.text: No award of damages is to be made unless, taking account of all the circumstances of the case... the court is satisfied that the award is necessary to afford just satisfaction to the person in whose favour it is made... In determining (a) whether to award damages, or (b) the amount of an award, the court must take into account the principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights in relation to the award of compensation under Article 41 of the Convention.
elements: Damages are discretionary, not automatic on a finding of breach
'Necessary' for just satisfaction is the threshold, considered alongside other relief already granted
Quantum must track Strasbourg Article 41 principles, not domestic tort measures

interaction.prompt: According to s 8(4), what must a court take into account when deciding whether to award damages and, if so, how much?
options: The principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights under Article 41
The damages that would be awarded for an equivalent tort at common law
Only the claimant's own assessment of the harm suffered
interaction.explanation: s 8(4) anchors quantum to Strasbourg's Article 41 'just satisfaction' principles — the whole reason Greenfield rejects reaching for tort-measure damages as the natural comparator.

parts.heading: Anufrijeva: damages as a remedy of last resort
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the principle out of the facts before naming it
body: Anufrijeva concerned a family whose asylum support was wrongly withdrawn and who alleged breaches of Article 8 arising from the way a local authority handled their case, including delay and poor administration. The Court of Appeal used the case to lay down general guidance on when damages are actually 'necessary' under s 8.

The central message: damages are not the default response to a finding of breach. Where a declaration that a right has been violated, or the practical outcome of the litigation itself (a benefit reinstated, a decision quashed), gives the claimant adequate vindication, no damages award is necessary at all. Maladministration alone — inefficiency, delay, poor process — will rarely cross the threshold unless it produces a distinct, quantifiable form of harm.

Students often read this as the courts being stingy for its own sake. It's better understood as institutional: s 8 damages sit within a public law remedial scheme, not a compensation scheme, and courts are consciously reluctant to turn every finding of maladministration into a quasi-tortious payout that would strain public authority budgets for harms that are often better and more cheaply remedied by simply putting things right going forward.

components.factsShort: A family's asylum support was withdrawn and their Article 8 rights were said to be breached by administrative delay and mishandling.
components.ratioShort: Damages under s 8 are a remedy of last resort: a declaration, or the substantive outcome of the case, will often provide adequate just satisfaction on its own.

expanded.facts: The claimants, a family seeking asylum, had their National Asylum Support Service accommodation and support withdrawn. They argued this, combined with prolonged administrative delay in resolving their situation, breached Article 8.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that damages should not be awarded routinely for maladministration; a finding of breach and the practical remedy secured by the litigation would, in most cases, constitute sufficient just satisfaction. Damages under s 8 are to be approached restrictively, reflecting Strasbourg's own modest approach to Article 41 awards.
expanded.significance: Anufrijeva is the leading domestic statement that s 8 damages are exceptional rather than routine — the default expectation should be that a declaration or a quashing order is enough, with damages reserved for cases where nothing less will do.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that damages under s 8 HRA are the routine, expected remedy once a breach is proven?
sliderLabels: Damages are routine on any proven breach
Damages are exceptional — a last resort
interaction.explanation: Anufrijeva is explicit: a declaration or the practical outcome of the case will often be adequate just satisfaction on its own. Damages are reserved for cases where nothing less will vindicate the right.

parts.heading: Faulkner: closing the gap with Strasbourg on quantum
parts.voice: direct — narrows in on the practical 'how much' question
body: Greenfield tells you the comparator is Strasbourg, not tort law. Faulkner tells you how closely domestic courts should track it. The Supreme Court considered damages claims arising from delayed Parole Board reviews of continued detention — a paradigm case where liberty was affected but no equivalent tort measure existed to reach for.

The Court held that domestic courts should be guided by, and broadly consistent with, the level of awards Strasbourg itself would be likely to make on comparable facts, while allowing for the fact that domestic courts are better placed to assess local circumstances in detail. This produced somewhat higher, more predictable awards than the most cautious post-Greenfield case law had suggested, without abandoning the 'just satisfaction' framework itself.

The exam-relevant takeaway is narrower than it sounds: Faulkner does not create a tort-style measure of damages. It refines the mechanics of applying the Strasbourg comparator — giving courts clearer permission to look closely at actual Strasbourg awards on similar facts, rather than treating the comparator as a vague gesture towards modesty.

components.label: Quantum: what changed and what didn't
points: Still no tort-measure damages — Greenfield's basic rule survives Faulkner intact
Courts should look closely at comparable Strasbourg Article 41 awards, not just gesture at 'modesty' in the abstract
Domestic courts may adjust for matters Strasbourg is less well placed to assess (e.g. detailed local evidence of impact)
The result was, in practice, a modest upward correction to some post-Greenfield awards — not a change of principle

interaction.prompt: Which scenario best reflects the Faulkner approach to assessing damages, rather than a Greenfield-era over-cautious approach?
interaction.scenarioA: A court finds a breach, notes that Strasbourg awards on similar facts cluster around a specific range, and assesses quantum closely by reference to that range while adjusting for detailed domestic evidence of impact.
interaction.scenarioB: A court finds a breach and awards a token, nominal sum simply because 'Strasbourg is generally modest', without examining what Strasbourg has actually awarded on comparable facts.
interaction.explanation: Faulkner's contribution is methodological: engage properly with comparable Strasbourg awards rather than defaulting to vague, token modesty. B reflects the kind of under-engaged reasoning Faulkner was decided to correct.

parts.heading: Choosing the right toolkit: HRA remedies vs judicial review
parts.voice: comparative — a reference part built for exam-strategy recall
body: By this point the shape of the HRA remedial scheme should be clear: narrow standing (s 7), discretionary and modest damages (s 8), and — where the problem is primary legislation itself rather than a public authority's act — the wholly distinct remedy of a declaration of incompatibility under s 4.

A declaration of incompatibility deserves its own note here because students routinely misdescribe it as a 'win'. It does not invalidate the legislation, does not benefit the claimant in their own case, and does not bind Parliament to change the law (s 4(6)). Its only guaranteed effect is triggering the possibility of a fast-track remedial order under s 10 — a discretionary, political response, not a judicial one.

Set this against ordinary judicial review, which offers a richer toolkit for unlawful public authority action generally — quashing orders, mandatory orders, prohibiting orders, and injunctions — available on a much wider range of grounds than a bare Convention breach, and with more generous standing rules. The practical skill this lesson is building is this: read the problem, identify what's actually wrong (an authority's decision, or the statute itself), and pick the remedy regime that fits — not the one you happen to have studied most recently.

components.title: Which remedy regime fits the problem?
components.description: A decision path for choosing between HRA remedies and judicial review relief.

nodes.label: Is the complaint about primary legislation itself, not how it was applied?
Yes → s 4 declaration of incompatibility (if a compatible reading isn't available under s 3)
No → is there an identifiable individual victim under s 7?
No individual victim → consider ordinary judicial review (generous standing) instead of a free-standing HRA claim
Yes → HRA claim available; consider s 8 damages only if declaration/other relief is inadequate to afford just satisfaction

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the complaint concerns primary legislation itself: if so, a s 4 declaration of incompatibility is the relevant remedy (assuming a compatible reading isn't available under s 3). If not, ask whether there is an identifiable individual victim under s 7: without one, ordinary judicial review — with its more generous standing rules — is the better route. With a victim, an HRA claim is available, but damages under s 8 should only be pursued where a declaration or other relief would not amount to adequate just satisfaction.

interaction.prompt: A statute's wording, on its plain terms, cannot be read compatibly with Article 8 under s 3. No individual claimant is yet affected — a campaign group wants to challenge it now, before it's applied to anyone. What is the most accurate advice?
options: A s 4 declaration of incompatibility can be sought by the campaign group directly, since it concerns primary legislation
A declaration of incompatibility requires a live case with an actual victim before the court — the group cannot bring a free-standing abstract challenge to the statute
The group should seek s 8 damages instead, since damages don't require a victim
interaction.explanation: s 4 declarations arise within proceedings brought by a victim under s 7 — there is no free-standing abstract-review route to a declaration of incompatibility. Without a victim, and without the statute yet being applied, the group has no HRA claim to attach the declaration to.

testPool.prompt: Name the two HRA sections that together structure this lesson's remedial framework.
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 7 (who may bring a claim — the victim test) and section 8 (what a court may award, including damages) together form the core remedial framework covered in this lesson.

testPool.prompt: Does s 7(7) HRA import a narrower or broader test of who can sue than 'sufficient interest' in judicial review?
options: Narrower — the Strasbourg 'victim' test
Broader — anyone with a genuine concern about the issue

testPool.prompt: Which of these best describes when a court MUST award damages under s 8 HRA?
options: Whenever a breach of a Convention right is established
Never — damages are always discretionary, awarded only if necessary for just satisfaction
Only when the claimant asks for damages specifically rather than a declaration
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option is the classic tort-law instinct this lesson exists to correct — a finding of breach never automatically triggers damages under s 8; necessity for just satisfaction is always assessed separately.

testPool.prompt: Under s 8(4), what must a domestic court do when assessing the amount of a damages award?
options: Take into account the principles the European Court of Human Rights applies under Article 41
Apply the same measure it would use for an equivalent tort claim
Award a fixed statutory sum set by the Ministry of Justice

testPool.prompt: Order the steps a court takes when deciding whether, and how much, to award under s 8.
items: Establish that a Convention right has been breached
Consider what other relief has already been granted (e.g. a declaration or quashing order)
Ask whether damages are necessary to afford just satisfaction
If necessary, assess quantum by reference to comparable Strasbourg Article 41 awards

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Greenfield, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on the measure of damages.
testPool.passage: The claimant argued that damages under s 8 should reflect the level a domestic tort claim would attract for a comparable wrong. The House of Lords rejected this approach. The correct approach is to apply the principles which the European Court of Human Rights itself applies when assessing just satisfaction under Article 41, not to import a tort measure of damages into a public law remedial scheme.
testPool.ratioSentence: The correct approach is to apply the principles which the European Court of Human Rights itself applies when assessing just satisfaction under Article 41, not to import a tort measure of damages into a public law remedial scheme.

testPool.prompt: Which claimant is more likely to recover damages under s 8, on Anufrijeva reasoning?
testPool.scenarioA: A claimant whose Article 8 breach caused prolonged, distinct and quantifiable harm that a declaration alone would not remedy or acknowledge adequately.
testPool.scenarioB: A claimant who experienced administrative delay and inefficiency, but whose situation was fully put right once the breach was identified and a declaration was made.
testPool.explanation: Anufrijeva treats mere maladministration, remedied by the practical outcome of the case, as insufficient to justify damages — A's distinct, unremedied harm is the kind of case where damages become 'necessary'.

testPool.prompt: A local authority unlawfully denies a family housing support in breach of Article 8. The family is rehoused within days once the error is caught, and a court declares the breach. On Anufrijeva principles, is a further damages award likely to be 'necessary'?
options: Unlikely — the declaration plus the practical remedy (rehousing) will usually be adequate just satisfaction absent further distinct harm
Certain — damages follow automatically once a breach is declared
Impossible — declarations and damages can never be combined
testPool.explanation: This tracks Anufrijeva directly: where the practical outcome plus a declaration gives adequate vindication, damages are not 'necessary' and should not be awarded as a matter of course.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you a s 4 declaration of incompatibility — not s 8 damages — is the relevant remedy here.
testPool.scenarioText: A claimant is refused a benefit because a statutory eligibility provision, on its plain wording, cannot be read compatibly with Article 14 even using s 3. No public authority acted unlawfully; they simply applied the statute correctly.
tappableSpans: cannot be read compatibly with Article 14
testPool.explanation: Once the authority has simply applied an incompatible statute correctly, the problem lies in the legislation itself, not in unlawful action by a public authority — that is precisely the territory of a s 4 declaration, not s 8 damages.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a declaration of incompatibility, once made, requires Parliament to change the offending statute?
sliderLabels: Parliament is not legally bound to change the law
testPool.correctPosition: Parliament is not legally bound to change the law
testPool.explanation: s 4(6) HRA is explicit: a declaration does not affect the validity of the provision and does not bind the parties to the proceedings. Any change is a political response via s 10 remedial order, not a legal obligation.

testPool.prompt: Aisha's Article 8 rights were breached when a local authority disclosed her confidential medical information without lawful basis. The disclosure caused her a distinct, ongoing reputational and psychological harm that a declaration alone would not remedy. Analyse whether she is likely to recover damages under s 8.
factsToOrder: The authority acted unlawfully under s 6 by disclosing the information
The breach caused distinct, ongoing reputational and psychological harm
A bare declaration would not adequately remedy that harm
Aisha is a direct victim under s 7

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Aisha, as a s 7 victim of an established Article 8 breach, is entitled to damages under s 8.
modelAnswer.rule: Damages under s 8 are discretionary and awarded only where necessary to afford just satisfaction, having regard to other relief granted and to Strasbourg Article 41 principles (s 8(3)–(4); Greenfield; Anufrijeva; Faulkner).
modelAnswer.application: Aisha is a direct victim with standing under s 7. The breach caused distinct, ongoing harm beyond what a bare declaration could vindicate, unlike the maladministration in Anufrijeva that was fully remedied by the practical outcome. Quantum should be assessed by close reference to comparable Strasbourg awards, per Faulkner, rather than a tort measure, per Greenfield.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Damages are likely to be 'necessary' here and recoverable, assessed by reference to Strasbourg comparator awards rather than domestic tort principles.

testPool.prompt: Does a declaration of incompatibility under s 4 quash or invalidate the offending legislation?
options: No — the legislation remains valid and in force
Yes — it is automatically repealed

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures what Faulkner changed relative to the strictest post-Greenfield case law?
options: It abandoned the 'just satisfaction' comparator and introduced tort-measure damages
It refined how closely courts should engage with comparable Strasbourg awards, producing somewhat higher and more consistent quantum without changing the underlying principle
It abolished damages under s 8 entirely in favour of declarations
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers both overstate the change — Faulkner is a methodological refinement of Greenfield's Strasbourg-comparator approach, not a reversal of it.

testPool.prompt: A pressure group, with no personally affected member, wants to challenge a Home Office policy as systemically unlawful and disproportionate under Article 8, for a wide class of unidentified people. Which route best fits?
options: A free-standing HRA claim under s 7, since the harm is serious
Judicial review, where standing rules are more generous and do not require the claimant itself to be a 'victim'
A s 4 declaration of incompatibility, since the policy is unlawful
testPool.explanation: Without an identifiable personal victim, s 7 blocks a free-standing HRA claim. Judicial review's more generous standing rules are the better-fitting toolkit for a systemic challenge brought by a representative body.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson is assuming a proven breach automatically produces a damages award. Under the HRA it almost never does on its own — check first whether a declaration or the practical outcome already provides adequate just satisfaction.
